text: The tokenizer hands the model a list of identifiers, and an identifier is only a name tag. The model turns each one into a vector with a remarkably simple device: a table with one row for every token in the vocabulary. Think of a cabinet of drawers, where the token's number tells you which drawer to open, and inside is a card holding a list of numbers. That card is the token's embedding, and looking it up is all the embedding layer does.

It helps to see the lookup as a matrix product, because that is how the rest of the network will treat it. Write the token as a one hot vector, a row of zeros with a single one at the token's position. Multiplying that row by the embedding table switches off every row of the table except one, so the product is exactly the row we wanted. Do this for a whole sentence at once and the rows stack up: a sequence of tokens becomes a matrix with one row per token and one column per embedding dimension. Keeping track of those two numbers, the sequence length and the width, will matter in every lesson that follows.

At first the table is filled with small random numbers, so the vectors point in arbitrary directions and mean nothing. Training changes that. Words that appear in similar company, like cat and kitten, have to help the model make similar predictions, so the gradient keeps nudging their rows in the same direction, while words used differently drift apart. Meaning is never written in by hand; it settles into the geometry because it is useful for predicting text.

Because meaning lives in direction, we compare two embeddings by the angle between them, using the cosine similarity you already know: the dot product divided by both lengths. Two arrows that point the same way score close to one, unrelated arrows score near zero, and the length of each arrow, which often reflects how frequent a word is, drops out of the comparison.

Directions can even carry relationships. In word vectors trained by an older method called word to vec, the step from man to woman points roughly the same way as the step from king to queen, so the difference between two words behaves like a reusable instruction. The effect is real but rougher than the famous example suggests, and it is best read as a hint that a learned space organises meaning along consistent directions.

Inside a language model, the embedding table is simply the first layer, learned together with everything after it, and each row is much longer than anything we can draw. The result is a matrix with a vector for every position in the text. The next question is how a model should read such a sequence, one vector after another, and that brings us to recurrent networks and why they struggled.
